slides.say: Given: x plus seven, in absolute value, is equal to nine. Which of the following could be the value of x?
So we have an equation with an absolute value, and all the choices are numbers. We'll solve it three ways, two cases, the number line, and plugging in the answers.
[short pause] Our first method, two cases. Remember, which numbers have an absolute value of nine? Nine, and negative nine. So the inside, x plus seven, is nine, or it's negative nine.
First case, x plus seven is nine. To get x alone, I take seven off both sides, and x is two.
Second case, x plus seven is negative nine. Take seven off again, and x is negative sixteen.
[short pause] Now careful with the choices. Is two there? No. But negative two is there, and that's the trap. It looks like our two, but it's a different number.

Negative sixteen is there, it's number three. And look at the wording, could be. Two values work, two and negative sixteen, but they only offer one of them. So negative sixteen, number three is our answer.

[pause] Our second method, the number line. What are we doing here? We read the bars as a distance. Remember, the absolute value of a number is its distance from zero. And the bars around a difference give the distance between two numbers. Five minus two is three, and from two to five is exactly three steps. Why? Five minus two tells me how far five is from two, and the sign only says which way. The bars drop the sign, so what's left is the distance. Now, x plus seven is x minus negative seven, because taking away negative seven is the same as adding seven. So x plus seven, in bars, is the distance between x and negative seven. And it's equal to nine, so x is exactly nine steps away from negative seven.
at: x plus seven is x minus

slides.say: So how do I read the picture? I start at negative seven, and I walk nine steps each way. Nine steps to the right, negative seven plus nine is two. Nine steps to the left, negative seven minus nine is negative sixteen. Those are the only two points that are exactly nine steps away. Two isn't in the choices, but negative sixteen is, choice number three.

[pause] And our third method, plugging in the answers. The choices are numbers, so let's just try them. Sixteen plus seven is twenty-three, and twenty-three isn't nine, so no. Negative two plus seven is five, and five isn't nine, so no again.
Negative sixteen plus seven is negative nine, and its absolute value is nine. It works. In the exam you'd circle it and move on.

So which way is better? The two cases are the standard way, and you'll need them in the harder questions. But when the choices are numbers, plugging in is just as fast. Bars equal to a number? Two cases, two answers. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: plugging in is just as fast
